claims.text: The baseline platinum-group-metal nanoscale catalyst has minimal surface hydroxyl or oxide coverage under ethanol-oxidation conditions.
Controlled potential-step treatments can induce a transient sub-monolayer of surface hydroxyl or oxide species.
The induced hydroxyl or oxide layer alters the catalyst surface electronic structure.
The altered surface electronic structure adjusts the binding energies of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Adjusted intermediate binding facilitates sequential electron and proton transfers during ethanol oxidation.
The induced surface state reduces catalyst poisoning caused by overly strong adsorption.
The induced surface state accelerates conversion of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Ethanol oxidation in the proposed regime involves twelve-electron and twelve-proton transfer.
Inducing the transient sub-monolayer enhances ethanol-oxidation activity relative to an untreated surface.
Inducing the transient sub-monolayer enhances ethanol-oxidation selectivity relative to an untreated surface.
Inducing the transient sub-monolayer enhances catalyst durability during ethanol oxidation.
The treated catalyst will have a lower ethanol-oxidation onset potential than the untreated baseline.
The treated catalyst will produce a higher ethanol-oxidation current density than the untreated baseline.
Operando X-ray absorption or Raman measurements will reveal hydroxyl or oxide signatures that correlate with improved ethanol-oxidation performance.
The proposed mechanism applies only over potential ranges that produce a sub-monolayer without forming a thick oxide.
Potentials or environments that cause excessive oxide formation can deactivate the catalyst.
The magnitude of the catalytic response may depend on catalyst morphology and electrolyte composition.
